definition: The smallest unit of an element that can exist. Atoms make up all matter and cannot be broken down by chemical reactions.
The tiny, dense centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons. It has a positive charge overall.
A positively charged subatomic particle found in the nucleus of an atom. Relative charge: +1, relative mass: 1.
A subatomic particle with no charge found in the nucleus of an atom. Relative charge: 0, relative mass: 1.
A negatively charged subatomic particle that orbits the nucleus in shells. Relative charge: -1, relative mass: very small (1/1836).
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. Also called the proton number. Determines which element an atom is.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom. Also called the nucleon number.
An energy level around the nucleus where electrons are found. The first shell holds up to 2 electrons, the second and third shells hold up to 8 electrons each.
The arrangement of electrons in the shells of an atom, written as a series of numbers (e.g. 2,8,1 for sodium).
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different mass numbers.
The weighted average mass of an atom of an element compared to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Takes into account the abundance of isotopes.
A charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons. Losing electrons forms a positive ion; gaining electrons forms a negative ion.
A substance made of only one type of atom. Cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded together in fixed proportions.
Two or more substances mixed together but not chemically combined. The substances can be separated by physical methods.
A table of all known elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number, grouped by similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row in the periodic table. Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells.
A vertical column in the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell and similar chemical properties.
An element found on the left and centre of the periodic table. Metals are typically shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, and have high melting points.
An element found on the right side of the periodic table. Non-metals are typically poor conductors, dull, and brittle as solids.
The Russian chemist who created the first widely accepted version of the periodic table in 1869, arranging elements by atomic mass and leaving gaps for undiscovered elements.
The elements in the first column of the periodic table (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr). They have one electron in their outer shell and are very reactive metals.
The elements in group 7 of the periodic table (F, Cl, Br, I, At). They have 7 electrons in their outer shell and are reactive non-metals.
The elements in the last column of the periodic table (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn). They have a full outer shell of electrons and are very unreactive.
The block of metallic elements in the centre of the periodic table (e.g. iron, copper, zinc). They are hard, dense, have high melting points, and can form coloured compounds.
How readily an element undergoes chemical reactions. In Group 1, reactivity increases down the group; in Group 7, reactivity decreases down the group.
A reaction where a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound. For example, chlorine displaces bromine from a bromine solution.
Group 1 metals react vigorously with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Reactivity increases down the group as the outer electron is further from the nucleus.
Halogens exist as diatomic molecules (e.g. Cl₂, Br₂). They get less reactive, darker in colour, and have higher boiling points going down Group 7.
Noble gases are monatomic (exist as single atoms), colourless, and have very low boiling points. They are inert (unreactive) because their outer electron shell is full.
An early model of the atom proposed by J.J. Thomson, where electrons were embedded in a sphere of positive charge, like plums in a pudding.
The model of the atom developed after Rutherford's gold foil experiment, showing a small, dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting around it.
A development of the nuclear model by Niels Bohr, proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels (shells) rather than random paths.
An experiment by Geiger and Marsden (directed by Rutherford) in which alpha particles were fired at gold foil. Most passed through, but some were deflected, leading to the nuclear model of the atom.
